Hook: A prosecutor wants convictions. A judge will convict only if guilt is more likely than not. Of every hundred defendants who come before them, 30 are guilty, and both know it. The prosecutor cannot lie, cannot hide evidence and cannot bribe anyone. The one thing she controls is which investigation to run: what will be looked at, and what will be reported. The judge sees the result, knows how the investigation was designed, and reasons correctly. How many defendants can she get convicted?

Three investigations. With none, the judge knows only that thirty percent are guilty. That is less likely than not, so everyone is acquitted. With a perfect investigation, the judge learns the truth, and the thirty guilty are convicted. Now a designed one. It flags every guilty defendant, and also flags 30 of the 70 innocent ones. Among the flagged, exactly half are guilty: just enough for the judge to convict, which a judge who follows the evidence must. 60 convictions out of a hundred: twice the truth, with nobody deceived. Emir Kamenica and Matthew Gentzkow called this Bayesian persuasion.

The question: how does someone who controls only what others learn get them to do what she wants? What do people infer from what they are shown? When does talk carry information, and how much? What is the best way to reveal, and what can it achieve? And what happens when many people learn from each other?
Economics, Built. Part fifty-three: information and persuasion.

This part is about information as a strategic object. Games in which players know different things, and equilibria with beliefs. Talk that costs nothing, persuasion by design, and information designed for many people at once. When one source of information is better than another for everyone; common knowledge; and global games. Herds, reputation, and bargaining when values are private. And promises that are kept only because the future matters.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: design the investigation.

Your turn. You design the investigation. It always flags a guilty defendant. You choose how often it also flags an innocent one. The judge, who knows that 30 percent are guilty and knows your design, convicts a flagged defendant only if, given what the flag means, guilt is at least fifty percent likely. Which design convicts the most: flagging none of the innocent, a fifth of them, three in seven, or sixty percent? Pause, and choose.

Here is every design. The more innocent defendants the investigation flags, the more defendants are flagged, so convictions rise: from thirty percent if it flags none of the innocent. But each innocent one flagged lowers what a flag means. The purple line is the judge's belief in guilt after a flag. At three innocent flagged for every seven, that belief is exactly one half, the judge still convicts, and 60 percent of defendants are convicted. Flag one more, and the belief falls below one half: the judge ignores the flag, and convictions fall to zero. The best design sits on the edge of the judge's willingness.

The arithmetic is Bayes's rule. The chance of guilt after a flag is the thirty percent who are guilty, all flagged, over everyone flagged. Set it equal to one half, and the innocent must be flagged three times in seven. Nobody is fooled: averaged over flags and no flags, the judge's beliefs are exactly right. But of those convicted, half are innocent: 30 defendants in a hundred. The prosecutor has used nothing but the judge's own standard of proof. That is the lever this part studies.
Bayesian: How do you play a game against someone whose payoffs you do not know? In three papers in 1967 and 1968, John Harsanyi gave the answer economics still uses. Imagine that nature moves first and draws each player's type: a firm's cost, a buyer's value, a defendant's guilt. Each player sees only their own type. A strategy says what every type would do. And in equilibrium, each type's action is a best response, on average over the types the others might be, using probabilities everyone shares. Incomplete information about payoffs becomes imperfect information about a move of nature, and ordinary game theory applies. This is a Bayes-Nash equilibrium.

An example: two firms competing in quantities, as in Part twelve, except that firm 1 does not know firm 2's cost. It is 4 or 1, equally likely; firm 1's own cost is 2. Firm 2 knows its cost, so it has two best-response lines: the orange one if its cost is high, the blue one if it is low. Firm 1 must choose one quantity that is best against the average of what the two types of firm 2 will do: the gold line. In equilibrium firm 1 makes 2.83, and firm 2 makes 1.58 if its cost is high and 3.08 if it is low. If firm 1 knew the cost, it would make 3.33 against a high-cost rival and 2.33 against a low-cost one. Not knowing, it hedges in between, and each type of firm 2 adjusts to that hedge.

How much is the missing information worth to firm 1? Not knowing, it expects a profit of 8.03. If it could learn firm 2's cost before choosing, 8.28. The difference is small here because firm 1's best choice moves only a little with what it learns; information is worth something only when it would change what you do. That idea returns in chapter seven, with Blackwell.
Dynamic: Chapter three. Beliefs on and off the path.

When moves happen in turn and some players know more, a later player learns from what an earlier one did. The equilibrium has to say what everyone believes. A perfect Bayesian equilibrium specifies a strategy for every player at every point where they move, a belief at every point about what has happened before, strategies that are best given those beliefs, and beliefs that follow Bayes's rule wherever it can be applied. The trouble is the points that are never reached in equilibrium. Bayes's rule says nothing there, and an odd belief about something that should never happen can hold up a strange equilibrium. Part thirteen met this with Spence's signals.

The classic example is In-Koo Cho and David Kreps's. A newcomer walks into a tavern. Ninety percent of newcomers are strong, the rest weak. The strong prefer beer for breakfast, the weak prefer quiche. A bully watches the breakfast and decides whether to pick a fight. He wins only against the weak, and avoiding a fight is worth more to the newcomer than the breakfast. One equilibrium: everyone has beer, and the bully, who learns nothing, does not fight. If he ever saw quiche, he would believe the eater weak and fight, so nobody eats quiche. A second: everyone has quiche, and the bully believes that whoever has beer is weak, so the strong swallow their quiche too. Both satisfy every rule so far.

Cho and Kreps asked which off-path beliefs are reasonable. In the quiche equilibrium, who could possibly gain by switching to beer? Not the weak: even without a fight, beer gives them 2, less than the 3 they get now. The strong could: beer without a fight would give them 3, more than 2. So the only sensible reading of a beer is that the drinker is strong, and the bully should leave him alone. But then the strong would switch, and the quiche equilibrium falls apart: it fails what they called the intuitive criterion. The beer equilibrium survives. The same test picks out the least costly separating equilibrium of Spence's education signals in Part thirteen.
CheapTalk: The prosecutor's investigation was a commitment: once designed, it reported what it found. What if there is no commitment, only talk? Vincent Crawford and Joel Sobel posed it in 1982. An adviser sees the state of the world, a number between zero and one. She sends a message: any words she likes, free and unverifiable. A decision maker hears it and acts, and wants his action to match the state. The adviser wants the action a little higher than the state, by a bias b: a financial adviser who earns more when you buy more, an agency that wants a bigger budget. If she would always exaggerate, why should he listen at all?

The answer is that he listens, but to coarse messages. In equilibrium the adviser does not report the state; she reports which of a few intervals it falls in, and the decision maker takes the action best for that interval. With a bias of 0.05, three messages: the state is below 0.13, between 0.13 and 0.47, or above. Notice that the intervals widen as the state rises: at the top, where she most wants to exaggerate, her words are least precise. With a smaller bias, more messages; with a larger one, fewer, and at a bias of a quarter or more, only one: nothing she says can be believed, and the talk is babble.

Here is the decision maker's expected loss in the most informative equilibrium, for every bias. It rises with the bias, with a kink each time one more message is lost, until it reaches the dashed line, what he would lose with no information at all. The more aligned the interests, the more talk can carry. That is why we ask about an adviser's incentives before we weigh her advice, and why commitment, the subject of the next chapter, can be worth so much.
Persuasion: Kamenica and Gentzkow's insight was to stop thinking about signals and think about beliefs. Before the investigation, the judge's belief in guilt is the prior, 0.3. After it, the belief is either zero, with no flag, or one half, with a flag. An investigation is nothing more than a way of splitting the prior into posterior beliefs. The only rule is that the posteriors must average back to the prior, weighted by how often each happens: zero with weight 0.4 and a half with weight 0.6 give 0.3. And any split that averages back to the prior can be produced by some investigation. So the prosecutor's question becomes: which split of beliefs is best for her?

Draw what the prosecutor gets at each belief the judge might hold. Below one half, nothing: the judge acquits. At one half or more, a conviction: the gold step. Now draw the smallest concave function that lies above it, the purple line, rising straight from zero to one at a belief of one half. The theorem: the best the sender can do at any prior is the height of the purple line there. At the prior of 0.3 it is 0.6, the sixty percent of the hook, achieved by splitting the prior between the two ends of that straight segment, zero and one half. Persuasion helps exactly when the purple lies above the gold at the prior. The method is called concavification; Robert Aumann and Michael Maschler used it in the 1960s for repeated games with private information.

The method works for any payoffs. Give the judge a middle verdict, a lesser charge, worth half a conviction to the prosecutor, chosen when the belief is between one third and two thirds. The concave closure changes shape, and at the prior of 0.3 it is 0.45. One best investigation splits the judge between certain innocence and a belief of one third, just enough for the lesser charge; splitting to two thirds, just enough to convict, does exactly as well here. With more than two states, beliefs live in a triangle or a higher simplex, and the same problem becomes a linear programme over candidate posteriors, which Agora solves.
Design: Chapter six. Information design for many.

Now the audience is not one judge but several people whose choices affect each other: depositors in a bank, buyers of a new asset, investors in a project. Dirk Bergemann and Stephen Morris built the theory. Take the simplest case. Two investors each decide whether to invest. The project is good forty percent of the time, when investing pays 1; when it is bad, investing pays minus 3. Each gains 1 more if the other invests too. A designer, a promoter or a regulator who wants the investment to happen, chooses what each investor is told.

Three policies. Tell them nothing, and each sees a project worth minus 0.4 on average even if the other invests: nobody invests. Tell them everything, and both invest when the project is good: 0.8 investors on average. The best design does twice as well. It sends both investors the same recommendation: invest whenever the project is good, and also 67 percent of the time when it is bad. An investor told to invest knows the project is good with just enough probability, and knows the other was told the same, so following the advice pays. Expected investment: 1.6.

The general method has a simple shape. Think of any information policy as recommending an action to each player, depending on the state. It works only if it is obedient: given what the recommendation reveals about the state and about what the others were told, each player wants to follow it. Bergemann and Morris called the outcomes Bayes correlated equilibria; finding the best one is a linear programme, which is how the numbers here were computed. Without a state, it is Robert Aumann's correlated equilibrium from Part eleven. The same arithmetic is used to think about what regulators should disclose about banks' stress tests, how ratings should be designed, and when alerts should sound.
Common: Everything so far assumed people share a prior and update by Bayes's rule. Robert Aumann drew a startling consequence in 1976. Take two people with the same prior who have seen different evidence. If their beliefs about some event are common knowledge, those beliefs must be equal. Common knowledge means that both know them, both know that both know, and so on without end. They cannot agree to disagree. Lasting disagreement between honest people needs different priors, or reasoning that is not Bayesian. That is a strong claim, so watch how it works.

John Geanakoplos and Heraklis Polemarchakis showed how agreement arrives. Nine equally likely states. The question is whether the state is 3 or 4; the truth is 1. Ann knows only which of three blue groups the state is in; Bob knows which of the pink groups. Ann sees states 1 to 3, one of which is in the event: she says one third. Bob sees 1 to 4, two of which are in the event: he says one half. But Ann's announcement told Bob something: had the state been 4, 5 or 6, she would have said one third as well, while a 7, 8 or 9 would have made her say zero. Each announcement rules states out, for both of them. Ann now reasons from what Bob said and says one third again; Bob, knowing what Ann's repeat rules out, comes round to one third. They agree, having exchanged nothing but their beliefs.

Common knowledge is demanding, and Ariel Rubinstein showed how much. Two generals should attack together, but only in a rare state of the world that one of them observes. He emails; the other's computer confirms automatically; that confirmation is confirmed, and so on, each email lost with a small chance, after which the exchange stops. A general who has seen some number of emails knows the last one he sent may have been lost, and puts probability 0.53 on the other having seen one fewer: more likely than not, however many were exchanged. The general who saw none will not attack. So one who saw one email, thinking it likely the other saw none, will not either; nor one who saw two; and so on up. Nobody ever attacks, even after a hundred confirmations. Almost common knowledge is not common knowledge, and coordination can depend on the difference.
Global: Bank runs in Part twenty-six and currency attacks in Part thirty-four both had two equilibria: if everyone runs, running is right; if nobody does, staying is. Which happens seemed a matter of sunspots. Take a regime, a currency peg, a bank, a government. Each speculator can attack at a cost of 0.4, and gains one if the regime falls. It falls if the share attacking exceeds its strength, theta. If theta is known to all, then for middling strength both all-attack and no-attack are equilibria. Hans Carlsson and Eric van Damme, and then Stephen Morris and Hyun Song Shin, changed one thing: each speculator sees the strength with a little private noise. Then there is only one equilibrium.

The argument fits on a card. Suppose everyone attacks when their signal is below some cutoff. Then the regime falls when its strength is below some threshold. The speculator whose signal is exactly at the cutoff must be indifferent: the chance that the regime falls, given her signal, equals the cost. And here is the beautiful step: from her point of view, the share of others attacking is equally likely to be anything between zero and one, whatever the noise. So the threshold is one minus the cost. With a cost of 0.4, the regime falls if and only if its strength is below 0.6. The sunspot is gone: the fundamentals decide, through what everyone thinks everyone else sees.

Uniqueness has a price: private information must be sharp relative to public information. Morris and Shin worked out the condition. Add a public signal that everyone hears, such as an official statement, and make it more and more precise. The curves show the equilibrium condition; each crossing with its dashed line is an equilibrium. With vague public information, one crossing. Sharper, still one. Sharp enough, and there are three: the multiplicity is back, because everyone now knows what everyone else knows. This is why central banks and regulators worry about what they say in public. A clear statement coordinates beliefs, for better or for worse.
Herds: Now let people learn from each other's actions instead of from a designer. In 1992 Abhijit Banerjee, and separately Sushil Bikhchandani, David Hirshleifer and Ivo Welch, showed how a crowd can go wrong with nobody making a mistake. Two restaurants, one better. Each diner gets a private hint that is right 70 percent of the time. Diners arrive one by one and see where the earlier ones went. The first follows her hint. So may the second. But once one restaurant leads by two choices, a diner's single hint cannot outweigh the lead, so she follows the crowd whatever her hint says, and so does everyone after her. Her choice reveals nothing, and learning stops. Four queues: most settle on the better restaurant; some lock onto the worse one within the first few diners, and never leave.

The arithmetic is exact. Count the hints that earlier choices have revealed, for the better restaurant minus against it; a cascade starts when the count reaches two either way. The chance of a cascade on the better restaurant rises quickly; the chance of one on the worse rises too; and the chance of still learning falls to almost nothing within a dozen diners. In the end 84.5 percent of queues are right, and 15.5 percent are wrong for ever, although the hints of the whole queue together would leave no doubt. Twenty thousand simulated queues agree with the formula.

How bad is it? The gold line is how often a long queue ends up right, against how good each hint is. The dashed line is a single diner on her own hint. Pooling everyone's hints would make the queue right almost surely. The herd does a little better than a lone diner and much worse than what the crowd collectively knows. The information is lost because actions are coarser than beliefs: once the herd forms, nobody's choice says what they saw. Reviews, ratings and fashions are attempts to keep that information flowing.
Reputation: Reputation is information about what someone will do. Reinhard Selten found a paradox in 1978. A chain store has branches in 20 towns. One by one, a local rival decides whether to enter. If one does, the store can fight a price war, which costs it, or accommodate, which costs less. In the last town there is no future to protect, so the store accommodates. Then, in the town before, fighting cannot deter the last entrant, so the store accommodates there too, and so on, all the way back. Every rival enters, and none is fought. Selten thought no real chain store would behave this way: surely it would fight the early entrants to deter the later ones.

David Kreps and Robert Wilson, and Paul Milgrom and John Roberts, resolved it with a little doubt. Suppose there is a 5 percent chance that the store is a kind that always fights, perhaps because its managers enjoy it. Then fighting is how an ordinary store keeps entrants guessing: its reputation is the entrants' belief that it is the tough kind. Early on, with many towns to come, even a small reputation is enough to deter entry: the grey line, the reputation needed, is tiny. Only near the end, in the last 4 towns, do entrants come in; and an ordinary store still fights with some probability to keep its reputation alive. A small doubt about one's type, and a long horizon, are enough to make a threat credible. The same logic explains why central banks guard their reputations for fighting inflation.
Bargaining: Bargaining is where private information hurts most. Start with the case without it. In 1950 John Nash asked what any sensible rule for splitting a surplus must satisfy. The curve is the set of deals that leave nothing on the table. Nash's axioms: efficiency; symmetry; independence of the units in which utility is measured; and that removing deals nobody chose should not change the choice. Only one rule satisfies all four: choose the deal that maximizes the product of the two gains, where the frontier touches the highest of these hyperbolas. Elegant, but it says nothing about how people actually get there.

Ariel Rubinstein modelled the haggling itself, in 1982. Ann makes an offer; Bob accepts or makes a counter-offer next round; every round of delay shrinks what is left. The game has exactly one subgame-perfect equilibrium, and in it the first offer is accepted at once. The first proposer's share depends only on the two players' patience. With equal patience it is one over one plus delta: two thirds when the discount is a half, and approaching one half as the delay between offers shrinks, which is where Nash's rule would put it. With complete information, there is no delay at all.

Add private information, and delay appears. A seller faces a buyer who values the good at 1 or 0.4, equally likely, over two periods. If the seller could commit, he would charge 1 and never cut the price. But he cannot: once the high-value buyer has bought, the only buyer left values the good at less, and the seller will cut the price. The high-value buyer foresees the cut and will pay only 0.52 today. The seller's best plan is to charge 0.52 now and 0.4 later, and the low-value buyer waits: a deal that both want is delayed, purely because of what the seller does not know. Ronald Coase argued that a monopolist selling a durable good, unable to commit, competes with its own future self.
Relational: The last idea is the oldest kind of incentive: a promise kept because the future matters. A firm promises a bonus for good work, but the quality of the work cannot be written into a contract a court would enforce. Once the work is done, the firm could simply keep the bonus. But then the worker leaves, or works badly from then on, and the firm loses the surplus of the relationship for ever. So the promise is credible if the bonus is no larger than the discounted value of the future: delta over one minus delta times the surplus each period. Clive Bull stated it in 1987; Jonathan Levin worked out the best such contracts in 2003.

In a simple version, effort produces output worth its amount and costs the worker half its square. The gold curve is the most effort a self-enforcing bonus can buy, against how much the future matters. The green line is what a contract a court would enforce could buy. Once the discount factor reaches 0.50, the promise is as good as a contract. Below that, the bonus that would be needed is larger than the future is worth, and effort falls in proportion. This is why long-term relationships, between firms and suppliers and between employers and staff, can do what contracts cannot, and why a shock that shortens horizons can unravel them. It is the repeated-game logic of Part eleven, put to work inside the firm.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: robust design and learning receivers.

The optimal investigation sat exactly on the edge of the judge's standard. That is its weakness. It was designed for a judge who convicts at a belief of one half. A slightly stricter judge, who needs 0.55, would see that a flag means only one half, and convict nobody. A designer unsure which judge she faces can aim at the stricter standard instead: 55 percent convicted, whichever judge it is. Robust design, which Dirk Bergemann and Stephen Morris began for mechanisms in 2005, gives up a little of the best case to avoid the worst. How much to give up, against audiences whose beliefs and standards are unknown, is an active field.

What remains open? Receivers who learn: an audience that watches a designer over many rounds learns her habits, and the receiver may itself be an algorithm. Robustness to audiences whose priors and standards the designer does not know. Attention: real receivers cannot read everything, and what they skip changes what a design can do; Part forty-five's rational inattention returns here. And measurement: how much people actually update, from persuasion rates in the field to beliefs elicited directly in surveys.
